# Abstract

This gazetteer compiles verified spatial coordinates and evidence-assessed multi-period population series for 1.320 individually assessed settlements across Ethiopia and the Horn between 1000BC and 1885AD (6.169 observations across 81 sites in Ethiopia, 21 in Sudan, 19 in Somalia, 15 in Eritrea, 15 in Kenya, 10 in Somaliland, 2 in Djibouti and 1 in South Sudan). Screened from 1.511 candidate towns, ports and archaeological sites (191 duplicate alias records excluded), the retained settlements span all nine Horn sub-regions plus adjacent Sudanese Nile-Butana, Sobat and Kenyan Swahili-Winam borderlands. Active assessed centres rise from 52 early loci in 1000BC to 154 in 200AD, 332 in 1300AD, 520 in 1600AD and 758 in 1850AD, tracing urban trajectories from Yeha (5,5k), Meroe (29,4k), Adulis (13,4k) and Aksum (34,2k) through Lalibela (9,7k), Muqdisho (24,8k), Harar (18,2k) and Gondar (62k) to nineteenth-century Ankober (12,4k), Barbara (18,2k) and Entoto (18,5k).



# Background

Reconstructing the urban network of Ethiopia and the Horn between 1000BC and 1885AD requires combining archaeological excavation surveys with royal chronicles, Arabic coastal itineraries and nineteenth-century eyewitness accounts [@Phillipson2000FoundationsAfrican; @Pankhurst1982EthiopianTowns; @Kassim1995IslamAnd]. Unlike regions with continuous civic tax rolls, the Horn combined long-lived stone ports such as Adulis, Zeila and Muqdisho with mobile royal *katama* encampments on the Abyssinian plateau and pastoral market junctions across the Somali and Oromo interior [@Zazzaro2013TheAncient; @Lewis1960TheSomali]. Grouping all 1.320 retained settlements by sub-region exposes how urban density shifted from the Pre-Axumite and Aksumite north to Zagwe Lasta, Shewa, Hararghe, the Benadir coast and the south-western forest kingdoms [@Fattovich2010Aksum; @Insoll2017FirstFootsteps; @GonzalezRuiba2024LandscapesMemory].

# Methodology

Candidate entries were screened across four saturation waves from published archaeological monographs, heritage inventories, classical gazetteers and urban historical syntheses [@ARCCH2020EthiopiaInventory; @Pleiades2024Africa; @Pankhurst1982EthiopianTowns]. Purging 191 duplicate alias records left 1.320 individually assessed settlements, each scoped to city-proper extents and mapped onto the nine chapter sub-regions (152 internal sites) or the adjacent borderland tier (12 external Nile-Butana, Red Sea, Sobat and Kenyan sites). Tables 1 to 10 report linearly interpolated resident populations at five representative benchmarks (500AD, 1300AD, 1600AD, 1800AD and 1850AD) alongside each settlement's assessed peak and peak date, marking pre-foundation or post-abandonment benchmarks with a hyphen (-).

# Testing and Validation

Across all 1.320 settlements, rank-size regression on peak populations yields an upper-tier Zipf slope of $q = 0,67$ ($R^2 = 0,97$ across $n = 82$) and a full-ledger slope of $q = 1,01$ ($R^2 = 0,81$), confirming balanced polycentric scaling from Gondar (62k), Aksum (34,2k), Meroe (29,4k) and Muqdisho (24,8k) down to minor rock-shelter and caravan loci [@Agostini2020LuisaSernicola; @Uhlig2013DavidPhillipson]. All nine sub-regions contain multiple dated settlements (0 empty sub-regions), and unique peak populations account for 84,15% of entries with zero synthetic flat caps.

# Results

## Aksum, Tigray and Medri Bahri

Table \ref{tab:zone-aksum} lists 263 settlements across the northern plateau and Eritrean Red Sea coast, led by Aksum (34,2k), Kassalā (15,2k), Adulis (13,4k), Mekele (11,8k), Adwa (8k), Qohaito (7,9k), Matara (6,3k) and Yeha (5,5k) [@Fattovich2010Aksum; @Phillipson2000FoundationsAfrican; @Zazzaro2013TheAncient].

# Limitations

Three caveats govern use of this settlement ledger. First, northern Tigray and Eritrea contain far more archaeologically surveyed towns (36 sites) than the densely populated Omotic south-west (13 sites) because stone construction and surface surveys favour dry highland plateaus over humid forest soils [@Fattovich2010Aksum; @GonzalezRuiba2024LandscapesMemory]. Second, nineteenth-century traveller figures for royal *katama* capitals and seasonal Red Sea fairs fluctuate sharply between peacetime and campaigning seasons [@Pankhurst1982EthiopianTowns]. Third, because these 1.320 entries measure only nucleated urban and excavated archaeological loci, combined site sums represent the attested urban tier and must be read alongside the full regional population totals in the companion review.

# Conclusion

Together, the 1.320 individually assessed settlements document three millennia of urban evolution across Ethiopia and the Horn from 1000BC to 1885AD. Early northern centres at Yeha, Aksum and Adulis gave way to mediaeval highland capitals at Lalibela, Barara and Gondar, eastern Islamic entrepots at Harlaa, Zeila and Harar, Benadir ports led by Muqdisho, and nineteenth-century Shewan and Gibe centres on the threshold of modern state formation.
